# 12-Week Vegan Muscle Gain Programme

## Client Overview

**Age:** 26 | **Goal:** Hypertrophy | **Diet:** Strict vegan | **Protein target:** 150 g/day | **Equipment:** Full gym access

---

## Programme Philosophy

The plan is divided into three four-week phases, each building on the last. Phase 1 establishes movement quality and a baseline training stimulus. Phase 2 increases volume and introduces more advanced loading techniques. Phase 3 pushes intensity to its peak before a brief deload in the final week. Training follows an upper/lower split across four sessions per week, leaving room for recovery, active rest, and adequate sleep — all of which are especially important for plant-based athletes whose protein synthesis rates can be slightly slower due to lower leucine density in many plant proteins.

---

## Nutrition Framework

### Daily Protein Target: 150 g from Plants Only

Because most plant proteins are lower in leucine and have incomplete amino acid profiles individually, the strategy is to **combine sources across the day** and **prioritise leucine-rich plant foods** at each meal. Aim for **four to five protein-containing meals or snacks** spread across the day, with no gap longer than four to five hours.

### Top Protein Sources to Rotate

| Food | Approx. Protein per 100 g cooked / per serving |
|---|---|
| Tempeh | 19 g per 100 g |
| Edamame | 11 g per 100 g |
| Firm tofu | 17 g per 100 g |
| Seitan (wheat gluten) | 25 g per 100 g |
| Lentils (red/green) | 9 g per 100 g cooked |
| Black beans / chickpeas | 8–9 g per 100 g cooked |
| Hemp seeds | 10 g per 30 g serving |
| Pea protein powder | 20–25 g per scoop |
| Brown rice protein powder | 20–22 g per scoop |
| Nutritional yeast | 8 g per 2 tbsp |
| Quinoa | 4 g per 100 g cooked |

### Sample Daily Meal Structure (≈150 g protein, ≈2,400–2,600 kcal)

**Meal 1 — Breakfast (≈35 g protein)**
Tofu scramble (200 g firm tofu, 17 g) + 2 tbsp nutritional yeast (8 g) + 1 cup edamame on the side (11 g) + oats with hemp seeds (10 g) = approx. 46 g. Adjust portions to appetite.

**Meal 2 — Pre-training snack (≈25 g protein)**
1 scoop pea protein shake blended with oat milk and a banana. Fast-digesting, easy on the stomach before training.

**Meal 3 — Post-training meal (≈40 g protein)**
200 g tempeh stir-fried with vegetables over 150 g cooked quinoa + 2 tbsp nutritional yeast. This is the most important meal of the day — consume within 60–90 minutes of training.

**Meal 4 — Afternoon/evening (≈30 g protein)**
Large lentil and black bean bowl (300 g combined cooked) with roasted vegetables and tahini dressing.

**Meal 5 — Evening snack (≈20 g protein)**
1 scoop brown rice protein mixed into a smoothie or stirred into oat porridge with nut butter.

### Key Micronutrients to Monitor

- **Creatine:** Not found in plant foods. Recommend **3–5 g creatine monohydrate daily** — this is one of the most evidence-backed supplements for muscle gain and is especially impactful for vegans who have lower baseline muscle creatine stores.
- **Vitamin B12:** Supplement daily (at least 250 mcg cyanocobalamin or 1,000 mcg every other day).
- **Vitamin D3 (vegan):** 1,000–2,000 IU daily from lichen-derived D3, especially in winter months.
- **Omega-3 (ALA → EPA/DHA):** Algae-based omega-3 supplement, 250–500 mg EPA/DHA daily. Supports inflammation management and recovery.
- **Iron and Zinc:** Prioritise lentils, pumpkin seeds, and fortified foods. Pair iron-rich foods with vitamin C to enhance absorption.
- **Iodine:** Use iodised salt or a supplement, as seaweed is inconsistent.
- **Calcium:** Fortified plant milks, tofu set with calcium sulphate, and leafy greens.

### Caloric Surplus

For muscle gain, aim for a **modest surplus of 200–350 kcal above maintenance**. If the client's maintenance is approximately 2,100–2,200 kcal (adjust based on actual TDEE assessment), target **2,300–2,550 kcal daily**. Track progress every two weeks and adjust upward by 100–150 kcal if weight is not moving.

---

## Training Programme

### Weekly Schedule Template

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Monday | Upper Body A (Push focus) |
| Tuesday | Lower Body A (Quad focus) |
| Wednesday | Active recovery / mobility |
| Thursday | Upper Body B (Pull focus) |
| Friday | Lower Body B (Posterior chain focus) |
| Saturday | Optional: light cardio, yoga, or extra mobility |
| Sunday | Full rest |

---

## Phase 1 — Foundation (Weeks 1–4)

**Goal:** Establish movement patterns, build connective tissue resilience, and create a baseline of volume the body can recover from. Rep ranges are moderate (8–12), loads are submaximal (RPE 6–7 out of 10), and rest periods are generous (90–120 seconds). This phase may feel conservative — that is intentional. Rushing into high volume without a foundation is the most common cause of stalled progress and injury.

---

### Week 1

**Monday — Upper A (Push Focus)**

Begin each session with 5–8 minutes of general warm-up (rowing machine or light cycling) followed by dynamic shoulder and thoracic mobility work.

- **Barbell Bench Press** — 3 sets × 10 reps @ RPE 6. Focus on controlled descent (3-second eccentric), full chest stretch at the bottom, and a strong lockout. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Dumbbell Overhead Press** — 3 sets × 10 reps @ RPE 6. Seated or standing. Keep core braced and avoid excessive lumbar extension. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Cable Chest Fly** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Light load, full range of motion, squeeze at the midline. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Tricep Pushdown (rope)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Elbows pinned to sides. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Lateral Raise (dumbbell)** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Controlled, no swinging. Rest 60 seconds.

**Tuesday — Lower A (Quad Focus)**

- **Barbell Back Squat** — 3 sets × 10 reps @ RPE 6. Prioritise depth and upright torso. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Leg Press** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Feet shoulder-width, full range. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Walking Lunges (dumbbell)** — 3 sets × 10 reps each leg. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Leg Extension** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Controlled extension and slow return. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Standing Calf Raise** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Pause at the top. Rest 60 seconds.

**Thursday — Upper B (Pull Focus)**

- **Barbell Bent-Over Row** — 3 sets × 10 reps @ RPE 6. Hinge at the hip, neutral spine, pull to lower sternum. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Lat Pulldown (wide grip)** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Full stretch at the top, pull elbows to hips. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Seated Cable Row (close grip)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Chest tall, retract scapulae. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Dumbbell Bicep Curl** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Supinate at the top. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Face Pull (cable)** — 3 sets × 15 reps. External rotation emphasis. Excellent for shoulder health. Rest 60 seconds.

**Friday — Lower B (Posterior Chain Focus)**

- **Romanian Deadlift (barbell)** — 3 sets × 10 reps @ RPE 6. Hinge deep, feel the hamstring stretch, drive hips forward. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Leg Curl (lying or seated)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Slow eccentric (3 seconds). Rest 90 seconds.
- **Hip Thrust (barbell)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Full hip extension, glute squeeze at the top. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Sumo Deadlift or Conventional Deadlift** — 3 sets × 8 reps @ RPE 6. Choose whichever feels more natural. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Seated Calf Raise** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Rest 60 seconds.

---

### Weeks 2–4

The structure remains identical to Week 1. Each week, apply **progressive overload** using the following simple rule: if all sets are completed with good form at RPE 6–7, add **2.5 kg to upper body barbell lifts** and **5 kg to lower body barbell lifts** the following week. If form breaks down, keep the weight the same and focus on quality. By Week 4, the client should be comfortably handling loads that feel like RPE 7 — working hard but with clear technique.

**Week 3 addition:** Introduce a **fourth set** on the two primary compound lifts per session (Bench Press, Squat, Row, RDL). This small volume increase prepares the body for Phase 2.

**Week 4 — Deload within Phase:** Keep all exercises the same but reduce load by 10% and drop to 3 sets × 8 reps across the board. This is not a rest week — it is an active recovery week that allows accumulated fatigue to dissipate before Phase 2 begins. Many clients feel stronger the week after a deload than they did going into it.

---

## Phase 2 — Volume Accumulation (Weeks 5–8)

**Goal:** Increase total weekly training volume — the primary driver of hypertrophy. Rep ranges shift to 8–15, RPE climbs to 7–8, and new techniques (supersets, drop sets on isolation work) are introduced. Rest periods on compound lifts remain 90–120 seconds; isolation work can be done with 60-second rests.

The split remains upper/lower but exercises are rotated to provide new stimuli and address any weaknesses identified in Phase 1.

---

### Week 5

**Monday — Upper A (Push Focus)**

- **Incline Barbell Bench Press** — 4 sets × 10 reps @ RPE 7. Incline shifts emphasis to upper chest and anterior deltoid. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Dumbbell Shoulder Press** — 4 sets × 10 reps @ RPE 7. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Cable Chest Fly (low to high)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Superset immediately with:
- **Incline Dumbbell Fly** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 60 seconds after the superset.
- **Overhead Tricep Extension (EZ bar or cable)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Lateral Raise** — 4 sets × 15 reps. Last set: drop the weight by 30% and continue for 10 more reps (drop set). Rest 60 seconds between sets.

**Tuesday — Lower A (Quad Focus)**

- **Barbell Back Squat** — 4 sets × 8 reps @ RPE 7–8. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Bulgarian Split Squat (dumbbell)** — 3 sets × 10 reps each leg. This is a demanding unilateral exercise — take time to find balance before loading. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Hack Squat or Smith Machine Squat** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Leg Extension** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Superset with:
- **Leg Curl** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Rest 60 seconds after superset.
- **Calf Raise (leg press machine)** — 4 sets × 20 reps. Rest 45 seconds.

**Thursday — Upper B (Pull Focus)**

- **Weighted Pull-Up or Assisted Pull-Up** — 4 sets × 8 reps. If bodyweight pull-ups are not yet achievable for 4 × 8, use the assisted machine or lat pulldown as a substitute. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Dumbbell Single-Arm Row** — 4 sets × 10 reps each side. Heavy, controlled. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Seated Cable Row (wide grip)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Hammer Curl (dumbbell)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Superset with:
- **Incline Dumbbell Curl** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 60 seconds after superset.
- **Rear Delt Fly (cable or dumbbell)** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Rest 60 seconds.

**Friday — Lower B (Posterior Chain Focus)**

- **Conventional Deadlift** — 4 sets × 6 reps @ RPE 7–8. Heavier and lower rep than Phase 1. Rest 2–3 minutes.
- **Romanian Deadlift** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Hip Thrust (barbell)** — 4 sets × 12 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Nordic Hamstring Curl or Lying Leg Curl** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Slow eccentric (4 seconds). Rest 90 seconds.
- **Glute-Ham Raise or Cable Pull-Through** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 60 seconds.

---

### Weeks 6–8

**Week 6:** Add one additional set to all compound movements (now 5 sets on primary lifts). Continue progressive overload on load where possible.

**Week 7:** Introduce **rest-pause sets** on one isolation exercise per session. After completing the final set, rack the weight, rest 15 seconds, then perform as many additional reps as possible. This technique increases effective volume without adding significant time.

**Week 8 — Deload:** Reduce volume by approximately 40% (drop back to 3 sets per exercise), reduce load by 10–15%, and keep RPE at 5–6. Prioritise sleep and nutrition this week. Protein intake should remain at 150 g — do not reduce food intake during a deload.

---

## Phase 3 — Intensification (Weeks 9–12)

**Goal:** Maximise intensity and push closer to muscular failure on key sets. Volume is slightly reduced compared to the peak of Phase 2, but intensity (RPE 8–9) and techniques such as mechanical drop sets, cluster sets, and tempo manipulation are used to drive further adaptation. This phase is demanding — recovery, sleep, and nutrition become even more critical.

---

### Week 9

**Monday — Upper A (Push Focus)**

- **Flat Dumbbell Bench Press** — 4 sets × 8 reps @ RPE 8. Dumbbells allow greater range of motion than a barbell. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Landmine Press or Arnold Press** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Cable Crossover (high to low)** — 3 sets × 12 reps @ RPE 8. Last set: reduce weight by 20% and continue to failure. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Close-Grip Bench Press** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Tricep emphasis. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Lateral Raise (cable)** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Cable provides constant tension throughout the range. Rest 60 seconds.

**Tuesday — Lower A (Quad Focus)**

- **Front Squat or Barbell Back Squat** — 4 sets × 6–8 reps @ RPE 8. If front squat is new, spend the first set at a lighter load to practise the rack position. Rest 2–3 minutes.
- **Bulgarian Split Squat** — 4 sets × 8 reps each leg @ RPE 8. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Leg Press** — 3 sets × 12 reps. On the final set, perform a **mechanical drop set**: complete 12 reps at full range, then immediately reduce range of motion to the top half and perform 8 more reps. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Leg Extension** — 3 sets × 15 reps, 3-second eccentric. Rest 60 seconds.
- **Calf Raise** — 4 sets × 15 reps. Rest 45 seconds.

**Thursday — Upper B (Pull Focus)**

- **Weighted Pull-Up** — 4 sets × 6 reps @ RPE 8. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Barbell Bent-Over Row** — 4 sets × 8 reps @ RPE 8. Rest 2 minutes.
- **Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Removes lower back fatigue, allowing full focus on the lats and rhomboids. Rest 90 seconds.
- **EZ Bar Curl** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Cluster set on the final set: perform 4 reps, rest 15 seconds, 4 reps, rest 15 seconds, 4 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Face Pull** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Rest 60 seconds.

**Friday — Lower B (Posterior Chain Focus)**

- **Deadlift (conventional or sumo)** — 4 sets × 5 reps @ RPE 8–9. This is the heaviest loading of the programme. Prioritise form above all else. Rest 3 minutes.
- **Romanian Deadlift** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Hip Thrust** — 4 sets × 10 reps @ RPE 8. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Lying Leg Curl** — 3 sets × 10 reps, 4-second eccentric. Rest 90 seconds.
- **Single-Leg Press** — 3 sets × 12 reps each leg. Rest 60 seconds.

---

### Weeks 10–11

Maintain the same exercise selection as Week 9. Continue progressive overload where possible — even small increases of 1.25 kg matter at this stage. In Week 10, push the final set of each compound lift to **RPE 9** (one rep in reserve). In Week 11, on two compound lifts per session, take the final set to **technical failure** — the point at which form would break down on the next rep. Do not go beyond this.

**Sleep and recovery note for Weeks 10–11:** Encourage the client to aim for **8–9 hours of sleep** per night. Growth hormone secretion peaks during deep sleep, and this is when the majority of muscle protein synthesis occurs. If sleep is poor, reduce intensity slightly rather than pushing through — training hard on poor sleep increases injury risk and cortisol levels.

---

### Week 12 — Final Deload and Assessment

This is not a rest week — it is a structured recovery week that allows the body to consolidate the adaptations made over the previous 11 weeks. Many clients will notice they look and feel their best in the week or two following a deload, as inflammation subsides and glycogen stores are fully replenished.

**Training:** Perform all four sessions but reduce to **3 sets × 8 reps** on all exercises at approximately **60–65% of the loads used in Week 11**. RPE should not exceed 6. Focus on movement quality, mind-muscle connection, and enjoying the training.

**Nutrition:** Maintain full protein intake (150 g). Carbohydrate intake can be slightly increased this week to ensure full glycogen replenishment — add an extra 50–75 g of carbohydrates per day from oats, sweet potato, or rice.

**Assessment:** At the end of Week 12, reassess the client using the same metrics taken at the start of the programme: body weight, circumference measurements (arms, chest, waist, hips, thighs), and performance benchmarks (working weights on squat, deadlift, bench press, and row). Progress photos taken in consistent lighting and posture are also valuable.

---

## Recovery Protocols

**Sleep:** Target 7.5–9 hours per night. This is non-negotiable for muscle gain. Poor sleep blunts anabolic hormone production and increases muscle protein breakdown.

**Active Recovery (Wednesday and Saturday):** Light walking, yoga, swimming, or a 20-minute foam rolling and stretching session. Keep heart rate below 120 bpm. The goal is to increase blood flow to muscles without adding training stress.

**Foam Rolling / Mobility:** Spend 10 minutes post-session on the muscles trained that day. Priority areas: thoracic spine, hip flexors, hamstrings, and lats.

**Stress management:** Chronic psychological stress elevates cortisol, which directly opposes muscle protein synthesis. Encourage mindfulness, journalling, or any stress-reduction practice the client enjoys.

**Hydration:** Aim for **2.5–3.5 litres of water per day**, increasing on training days. Adequate hydration supports nutrient transport, joint lubrication, and performance.

## Progress Tracking Recommendations

- **Weigh in** twice per week (same time, same conditions — morning, after using the bathroom, before eating). Average the two readings. Expect 0.25–0.5 kg of weight gain per month as a realistic, lean muscle gain target.
- **Log all training sessions** — weight used, sets, reps, and a brief RPE note. This is the most important tool for ensuring progressive overload is actually happening.
- **Photograph every four weeks** under consistent conditions.
- **Measure circumferences** at Weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12.
- **Review nutrition** every two weeks. If weight is not increasing after two weeks, add 150–200 kcal per day. If weight is increasing faster than 0.5 kg per week, reduce by 100–150 kcal.

# Cardio Addition — 12-Week Vegan Muscle Gain Programme

## Cardio Philosophy for a Muscle Gain Goal

Before prescribing cardio, it is important to be transparent with the client about the relationship between cardiovascular training and hypertrophy. Cardio and resistance training send partially competing signals to the body — resistance training drives the mTOR pathway (muscle building), while sustained aerobic work activates AMPK (energy conservation and endurance adaptation). This does not mean cardio should be avoided; it means it needs to be **dosed carefully and strategically** so that it supports the programme rather than undermining it.

For this client, cardio serves four specific purposes:

1. **Cardiovascular health and general fitness** — a recreational lifter should not neglect her aerobic base.
2. **Appetite and nutrient partitioning** — moderate cardio can improve insulin sensitivity, helping nutrients be directed toward muscle rather than fat.
3. **Recovery** — low-intensity cardio on rest days increases blood flow to muscles, accelerating clearance of metabolic waste products.
4. **Caloric management** — because she is eating in a surplus, a modest cardio load helps ensure the surplus remains lean rather than excessive.

The guiding rules are: **keep most cardio low intensity, keep sessions short, never place high-intensity cardio the day before a heavy leg session, and account for cardio calories in her nutrition targets.**

---

## Cardio Calorie Compensation

This is the most commonly overlooked element when adding cardio to a muscle gain programme. If the client burns an additional 150–300 kcal per session through cardio and does not eat more, she risks slipping out of her caloric surplus and stalling muscle growth. For every cardio session performed, she should add approximately **half to two-thirds of the estimated calories burned** back into her daily food intake, prioritising carbohydrates and protein. A practical rule of thumb: add an extra **half cup of oats or a medium sweet potato and a small protein source** on cardio days.

---

## Cardio Types Used in This Programme

**LISS — Low-Intensity Steady State**
Heart rate maintained at **60–70% of maximum heart rate (HRmax)**. For a 26-year-old, HRmax is approximately 194 bpm, making the LISS target zone **116–136 bpm**. This intensity is conversational — she should be able to speak in full sentences. Options include incline treadmill walking, light cycling, elliptical, or rowing at an easy pace. LISS is the primary cardio tool in this programme because it causes minimal interference with muscle protein synthesis and aids recovery.

**MISS — Moderate-Intensity Steady State**
Heart rate at **70–80% HRmax**, approximately **136–155 bpm**. Breathing is elevated but sustainable. Used sparingly and only on days well separated from heavy leg training.

**HIIT — High-Intensity Interval Training**
Heart rate reaching **85–95% HRmax** during work intervals. HIIT is the most time-efficient cardio format but also the most taxing on the muscular and nervous system. For this reason it is introduced only in Phase 2, kept to one session per week maximum, and never placed adjacent to lower body training days. HIIT sessions in this programme are short — 15–20 minutes of work intervals only, not including warm-up and cool-down.

---

**Total weekly cardio volume:** approximately **55–85 minutes** depending on phase. This is deliberately modest. More is not better when the primary goal is muscle gain.

---

## Phase-by-Phase Cardio Prescription

---

### Phase 1 — Foundation (Weeks 1–4)

**Cardio goal this phase:** Establish the habit, build aerobic base, keep intensity low, and ensure cardio never compromises recovery from resistance training. The client's body is adapting to a new training stimulus in the gym — do not overload the recovery system simultaneously.

**Week 1**

- **Monday post-session:** 15 minutes LISS on the treadmill at an incline of 4–6%, speed 5–6 km/h. Heart rate should settle at 120–130 bpm. This serves as an extended cool-down as much as a cardio stimulus.
- **Wednesday:** 25 minutes LISS on the stationary bike or elliptical. Maintain a comfortable, rhythmic pace. Use this session to decompress mentally as well as physically — no phone, focus on breathing.
- **Thursday post-session:** 15 minutes LISS on the rowing machine at a light pace. The rowing machine is particularly useful here because it gently moves the upper body through a pulling pattern, promoting blood flow to the muscles just trained.
- **Saturday:** 20 minutes LISS — walking outdoors counts. Fresh air and natural light have measurable benefits for sleep quality and mood, both of which support muscle gain.

**Total Week 1 cardio:** approximately 75 minutes at low intensity.

**Weeks 2–4:** The structure remains identical to Week 1. Do not increase duration or intensity during Phase 1. The temptation to do more is common — resist it. The resistance training volume is already increasing week on week, and the body needs its recovery resources directed there. Consistency at low intensity across four weeks will build a meaningful aerobic base without any interference effect.

**Week 4 deload adjustment:** During the deload week, cardio sessions can be extended slightly if the client feels good — Wednesday LISS can go to 35 minutes, and Saturday to 30 minutes. Because resistance training load is reduced, there is more recovery capacity available.

---

### Phase 2 — Volume Accumulation (Weeks 5–8)

**Cardio goal this phase:** Introduce moderate intensity on one session per week and add one short HIIT session. Total cardio time increases slightly but remains controlled. The client should be eating more to compensate for both the increased training volume and the additional cardio.

**Week 5**

- **Monday post-session:** 15 minutes LISS. Same as Phase 1 — this is a consistent habit now.
- **Wednesday:** 30 minutes MISS on the treadmill or bike. Heart rate target 136–150 bpm. This is the first time intensity increases. She should feel like she is working but could sustain this pace for a long time. If heart rate climbs above 155 bpm, slow down.
- **Thursday post-session:** 15 minutes LISS on the rowing machine or elliptical.
- **Saturday:** **20 minutes HIIT** (plus 5-minute warm-up and 5-minute cool-down). See HIIT protocol below.

**Total Week 5 cardio:** approximately 80 minutes, mixed intensity.

**HIIT Protocol — Saturday Sessions (Phase 2 and 3)**

Perform on the stationary bike, treadmill, or rowing machine. The bike is recommended as the first choice because it is lower impact and places less eccentric stress on the legs than treadmill sprints.

*Warm-up:* 5 minutes easy cycling or walking, gradually increasing pace.

*Work intervals:* 20 seconds at maximum sustainable effort (RPE 9 — very hard, cannot speak), followed by 40 seconds of very easy pedalling or slow walking. Repeat for **10 rounds** in Weeks 5–6, building to **12 rounds** in Weeks 7–8. Total work time: 10–12 minutes of intervals within the session.

*Cool-down:* 5 minutes easy movement, then 5 minutes of static stretching focusing on hip flexors, quads, and calves.

**Important:** If the client reports that her legs feel heavy or sore going into Monday's session after Saturday HIIT, move HIIT to Thursday post-session instead and make Saturday a LISS day. Individual recovery varies — adjust accordingly.

**Weeks 6–8 progression:**

- **Week 6:** Wednesday MISS increases to 35 minutes. HIIT rounds increase to 11.
- **Week 7:** Wednesday MISS increases to 40 minutes. HIIT rounds increase to 12. Saturday MISS option: if the client is recovering well, she can replace Saturday HIIT with 30 minutes of MISS for a change of stimulus.
- **Week 8 (deload):** Drop all cardio back to LISS only. Wednesday 30 minutes, Monday and Thursday 15 minutes post-session, Saturday 25 minutes. No HIIT this week. This is a full recovery week for both the muscular and cardiovascular systems.

---

### Phase 3 — Intensification (Weeks 9–12)

**Cardio goal this phase:** Resistance training intensity is at its peak, so cardio volume is deliberately held steady or slightly reduced compared to the peak of Phase 2. The priority is ensuring the client can recover fully between resistance sessions. HIIT is maintained but not increased. LISS remains the backbone.

**Week 9**

- **Monday post-session:** 15 minutes LISS. Incline treadmill walk.
- **Wednesday:** 35 minutes LISS. Drop back from the MISS of Phase 2 — the heavier lifting this phase means the Wednesday session should be genuinely easy. Heart rate no higher than 130 bpm.
- **Thursday post-session:** 15 minutes LISS.
- **Saturday:** 20 minutes HIIT (12 rounds, 20 seconds on / 40 seconds off) on the bike. Keep this session sharp and focused. Because resistance training RPE is now 8–9, the body is under significant stress — the HIIT session should feel hard but should not leave her feeling depleted for days afterward. If it does, reduce to 10 rounds.

**Total Week 9 cardio:** approximately 85 minutes, mixed intensity.

**Weeks 10–11:**

Maintain the exact same cardio structure as Week 9. Do not add volume or intensity. The resistance training is doing the heavy lifting (literally) in these weeks. Cardio is maintenance only. If the client reports feeling run down, fatigued, or notices her performance in the gym declining, the first adjustment is to remove the Saturday HIIT session and replace it with 25 minutes of LISS or a full rest day.

**Signs that cardio volume is too high for this individual:**
- Persistent muscle soreness that does not resolve between sessions
- Declining strength or reps in the gym week on week
- Poor sleep despite adequate hours in bed
- Increased resting heart rate (if she tracks this)
- Low mood or motivation

If two or more of these signs appear simultaneously, reduce cardio by removing one session entirely for one week before reassessing.

**Week 12 (Final Deload):**

- **Monday post-session:** 10 minutes very easy LISS.
- **Wednesday:** 30 minutes LISS outdoors if possible — a walk or light jog in fresh air. This is as much about mental recovery and reflection as physical.
- **Thursday post-session:** 10 minutes very easy LISS.
- **Saturday:** 20–25 minutes LISS. Enjoy it. The hard work is done.
- **No HIIT in Week 12.**

## Cardio Equipment Rotation

Rotating equipment across the week prevents overuse stress on any single joint and keeps sessions mentally fresh.

- **Monday:** Incline treadmill walk (LISS)
- **Wednesday:** Stationary bike or elliptical (LISS / MISS)
- **Thursday:** Rowing machine (LISS) — excellent full-body recovery tool
- **Saturday:** Stationary bike (HIIT in Phase 2–3) or outdoor walk (LISS)

---

## Heart Rate Monitoring

Encourage the client to use a heart rate monitor or fitness watch during cardio sessions, at least initially, to learn what each intensity zone actually feels like. Many people significantly underestimate or overestimate their effort without objective feedback. After four to six weeks, most clients develop a reliable sense of their zones by feel alone — but the data in the early weeks is invaluable for calibrating effort correctly.

---

*All cardio prescriptions should be adjusted based on the client's individual recovery, sleep quality, and gym performance. If strength numbers are moving in the right direction and the client feels energised, the cardio load is appropriate. If either of those things stalls, cardio is the first variable to reduce before touching the resistance programme.*

# Post-Workout Meal Suggestions

## Principles First

Before the meal ideas, it helps to understand what a post-workout meal needs to accomplish for this specific client, because those requirements shape every suggestion below.

**Protein:** The post-workout window is the period of greatest muscle protein synthesis sensitivity. She needs a meal delivering at least **35–45 g of complete protein** — meaning all nine essential amino acids are present, with particular emphasis on **leucine**, the amino acid that most directly triggers the mTOR muscle-building pathway. This is the biggest nutritional challenge for a vegan lifter, because most individual plant proteins are either leucine-poor or incomplete. The solution is **strategic combination** — pairing sources so that together they cover the full amino acid spectrum and hit an adequate leucine threshold (approximately 2.5–3 g of leucine per meal).

**Carbohydrates:** Resistance training depletes muscle glycogen. Replenishing it post-workout is important not just for energy but because insulin — released in response to carbohydrates — is itself anabolic and helps shuttle amino acids into muscle cells. Aim for **60–90 g of carbohydrates** in the post-workout meal, favouring moderate to high glycaemic index sources immediately after training when glycogen resynthesis is fastest.

**Fat:** Keep fat relatively low in the immediate post-workout meal — **under 15–20 g** — because fat slows gastric emptying and delays the arrival of amino acids and glucose into the bloodstream. Fat is not harmful post-workout, but it is not the priority here.

**Timing:** Aim to eat within **60–90 minutes** of finishing training. The anabolic window is not as narrow as was once believed, but eating sooner rather than later is still the better habit, particularly for a client training four days per week where recovery between sessions is important.

**Digestibility:** Some high-fibre plant foods, while nutritionally excellent, can cause bloating or discomfort when eaten in large quantities immediately after training. The meals below are designed with digestibility in mind — whole foods are prioritised but fibre load is moderated in the immediate post-workout context.

---

## The Meals

---

### Meal 1 — Tempeh and Sweet Potato Power Bowl

**Why it works:** Tempeh is one of the best post-workout proteins in a vegan diet. Unlike many plant proteins, it is fermented, which improves digestibility and bioavailability significantly. It is also one of the highest-leucine plant foods available. Sweet potato provides fast-replenishing carbohydrates with a good glycaemic response, and the combination of tempeh with edamame creates a very complete amino acid profile.

**Ingredients:**
- 200 g tempeh, sliced and pan-fried in 1 tsp coconut oil with soy sauce and garlic
- 250 g sweet potato, roasted or microwaved and mashed
- 100 g edamame, steamed
- Large handful of spinach, wilted in the pan
- 1 tbsp nutritional yeast stirred through the sweet potato
- Squeeze of lemon juice and chilli flakes to taste

**Approximate macros:**
- Protein: **42 g**
- Carbohydrates: **72 g**
- Fat: **14 g**
- Calories: **~580 kcal**

**Prep tip:** Tempeh can be batch-cooked at the start of the week and refrigerated. After training, simply reheat in a pan for three to four minutes while the sweet potato microwaves. Total prep time post-workout is under ten minutes.

---

### Meal 2 — Pea Protein and Oat Smoothie Bowl

**Why it works:** This is the fastest option on the list — ideal for days when appetite is low immediately after training or time is short. Blending breaks down cell walls and removes the chewing and digestion burden, meaning amino acids reach the bloodstream quickly. Oats provide a sustained carbohydrate release, and the banana adds fast-acting sugars for immediate glycogen replenishment. The combination of pea protein and hemp seeds creates a more complete amino acid profile than pea protein alone.

**Ingredients:**
- 2 scoops pea protein powder (vanilla or unflavoured) — approximately 44–50 g protein
- 1 large frozen banana
- 80 g rolled oats, blended into the smoothie or served as a base
- 250 ml oat milk or soy milk (soy milk adds an extra 6–8 g protein)
- 2 tbsp hemp seeds
- 1 tbsp almond butter (keep this modest to manage fat content)
- Handful of frozen mango or berries for carbohydrates and antioxidants
- Blend and pour over the oats if making a bowl, or drink as a shake

**Approximate macros:**
- Protein: **48 g**
- Carbohydrates: **78 g**
- Fat: **16 g**
- Calories: **~620 kcal**

**Prep tip:** Pre-portion the dry ingredients (protein powder, oats, hemp seeds) into a container the night before. After training, add the frozen fruit and liquid and blend. This is genuinely a five-minute meal.

---

### Meal 3 — Tofu Fried Rice

**Why it works:** This is a satisfying, warm, savoury meal that works particularly well after evening training sessions when the client wants something substantial. Firm tofu pressed and pan-fried until golden has a much better texture than soft tofu and a higher protein density per gram. White rice is used here rather than brown — post-workout is one of the few times where a faster-digesting carbohydrate source is preferable, and white rice is easier on the digestive system after intense exercise.

**Ingredients:**
- 250 g firm tofu, pressed for at least 15 minutes, cubed and pan-fried until golden
- 200 g cooked white rice (approximately 80 g dry weight)
- 100 g frozen peas and corn, added to the pan
- 2 tbsp low-sodium soy sauce or tamari
- 1 tsp sesame oil (added at the end — small amount for flavour)
- 3 spring onions, sliced
- 1 tsp fresh ginger, grated
- 2 tbsp nutritional yeast stirred through at the end
- Optional: 1 tbsp sriracha

**Approximate macros:**
- Protein: **38 g**
- Carbohydrates: **68 g**
- Fat: **12 g**
- Calories: **~540 kcal**

**Prep tip:** Cook a large batch of white rice at the start of the week and refrigerate it. Day-old rice actually fries better than freshly cooked rice because it is drier. After training, this meal takes approximately eight minutes from fridge to plate.

---

### Meal 4 — Seitan and White Bean Wrap

**Why it works:** Seitan is the highest-protein plant food by weight — up to 25 g per 100 g — making it an extremely efficient post-workout protein source. Combining it with white beans adds lysine, an amino acid that wheat gluten is notably low in, creating a much more complete protein profile. The wrap provides fast carbohydrates, and the overall meal is portable and easy to eat on the go if the client trains away from home.

**Ingredients:**
- 150 g seitan, sliced and pan-fried with smoked paprika, cumin, and garlic powder
- 100 g white beans (cannellini or butter beans), lightly mashed with lemon juice and salt
- 2 large flour tortillas or wraps
- Large handful of rocket or mixed leaves
- 4 tbsp salsa or tomato-based sauce
- Sliced avocado — half an avocado (note: this brings fat up slightly, so keep the portion modest)
- 1 tbsp nutritional yeast mixed into the bean mash

**Approximate macros:**
- Protein: **45 g**
- Carbohydrates: **74 g**
- Fat: **18 g**
- Calories: **~630 kcal**

**Prep tip:** Seitan can be purchased pre-made from most health food stores or supermarkets, or made in bulk at home from vital wheat gluten flour. The bean mash can be prepared in advance and refrigerated for up to four days. Assembly takes under five minutes.

**Note:** Seitan is not suitable if the client has coeliac disease or non-coeliac gluten sensitivity. If this applies, substitute with tempeh or tofu.

---

### Meal 5 — Red Lentil Dal with Basmati Rice

**Why it works:** Red lentils are one of the most digestible legumes — they are split, meaning they cook quickly and are much easier on the gut than whole legumes. They are also relatively high in leucine for a plant food. Paired with basmati rice, this creates a complete amino acid profile (the classic legume-plus-grain combination), and the meal is warm, comforting, and anti-inflammatory thanks to the turmeric and ginger. This works especially well as a post-workout dinner.

**Ingredients:**
- 150 g dry red lentils, rinsed and cooked (yields approximately 300 g cooked)
- 180 g dry basmati rice, cooked (yields approximately 360 g cooked)
- 1 tin chopped tomatoes
- 1 medium onion, diced and sautéed
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp garam masala, half tsp chilli powder
- 1 tsp fresh ginger, grated
- 200 ml light coconut milk (adds creaminess without excessive fat)
- Large handful of spinach stirred in at the end
- Fresh coriander to serve

**Approximate macros:**
- Protein: **36 g**
- Carbohydrates: **88 g**
- Fat: **10 g**
- Calories: **~580 kcal**

**Prep tip:** Dal improves with time and reheats beautifully. Make a large pot on Sunday and refrigerate in portions. After training, reheat in three minutes and serve over freshly cooked rice. This is one of the most cost-effective and nutritionally dense post-workout meals on the list.

---

### Meal 6 — Edamame and Quinoa Protein Salad

**Why it works:** This is the best option for clients who prefer not to eat hot food after training, or who train in warmer months when a cold meal is more appealing. Quinoa is one of the few plant foods that is a complete protein on its own, and edamame is exceptionally high in leucine relative to other plant proteins. Together they create a very strong amino acid profile. This meal is also high in micronutrients — iron, magnesium, zinc, and folate — which are all important for a vegan athlete.

**Ingredients:**
- 180 g dry quinoa, cooked and cooled (yields approximately 400 g cooked)
- 200 g shelled edamame, steamed
- 100 g chickpeas, rinsed from a tin
- Large handful of cherry tomatoes, halved
- Half a cucumber, diced
- 1 red pepper, diced
- 3 tbsp pumpkin seeds
- 2 tbsp nutritional yeast

**Dressing:**
- 2 tbsp tahini
- Juice of 1 lemon
- 1 clove garlic, minced
- 1 tsp maple syrup
- Water to thin to desired consistency
- Salt and pepper

**Approximate macros:**
- Protein: **40 g**
- Carbohydrates: **70 g**
- Fat: **18 g**
- Calories: **~600 kcal**

**Prep tip:** This entire salad can be made in advance and stored in the fridge for up to three days. Keep the dressing separate until ready to eat. After training, simply portion into a bowl, drizzle with dressing, and eat. Zero cooking required post-workout.

---

### Meal 7 — Soy Milk Protein Porridge

**Why it works:** This is the ideal option for clients who train early in the morning and want something warm, quick, and easy to digest before starting their day. Soy milk is used specifically here rather than oat or almond milk because it is the only plant milk with a protein content comparable to dairy milk — approximately 6–8 g per 250 ml — and it has a complete amino acid profile. The addition of protein powder and hemp seeds brings the total protein to a meaningful post-workout level without the meal feeling heavy.

**Ingredients:**
- 100 g rolled oats
- 400 ml unsweetened soy milk, used as the cooking liquid
- 1 scoop pea or brown rice protein powder, stirred in after cooking
- 2 tbsp hemp seeds
- 1 tbsp almond or peanut butter
- 1 medium banana, sliced on top
- 1 tbsp maple syrup or a few medjool dates for sweetness
- Cinnamon and a pinch of salt

**Approximate macros:**
- Protein: **38 g**
- Carbohydrates: **80 g**
- Fat: **16 g**
- Calories: **~610 kcal**

**Prep tip:** Overnight oats work perfectly here — combine oats and soy milk the night before and refrigerate. In the morning after training, stir in the protein powder (which dissolves better into cold oats than hot), add toppings, and eat. Alternatively, cook on the hob in five minutes.

Dietary variety is important for a vegan athlete for two reasons beyond simple enjoyment: different plant proteins have different amino acid strengths and weaknesses, so rotating sources across the week ensures a broader spectrum of amino acids overall; and different whole foods bring different micronutrient profiles, reducing the risk of any single deficiency developing over time.

# Protein Powder Recommendations for a Vegan Client

## How to Evaluate a Vegan Protein Powder

Before naming specific products, it is worth giving you a framework for evaluating any protein powder you come across, because the market changes constantly and regional availability varies. A good vegan protein powder for a muscle gain goal should meet the following criteria.

**Amino acid completeness:** This is the most important factor. A single-source plant protein will almost always have at least one limiting amino acid — the one present in insufficient quantity to support full muscle protein synthesis. Pea protein is low in methionine and cysteine. Rice protein is low in lysine. Hemp protein is low in lysine and leucine. A **blended protein powder** combining two or more sources overcomes this limitation and is almost always the better choice over a single-source product for a muscle gain goal.

**Leucine content:** As discussed in the nutrition framework, leucine is the primary trigger for muscle protein synthesis via the mTOR pathway. A good post-workout protein powder should deliver at least **2.5 g of leucine per serving**. Check the amino acid profile on the label or manufacturer website — reputable brands publish this. Pea protein is relatively leucine-rich for a plant source (approximately 1.8–2.2 g per 25 g serving), which is why it forms the backbone of most good vegan blends.

**Protein per serving:** Look for at least **20–25 g of protein per serving** with a relatively low calorie cost — ideally under 150 kcal per scoop. This ensures the powder is doing its job efficiently without adding unnecessary calories that make hitting the overall dietary targets harder.

**PDCAAS or DIAAS score:** These are the two scientific measures of protein quality. PDCAAS (Protein Digestibility Corrected Amino Acid Score) and the newer DIAAS (Digestible Indispensable Amino Acid Score) both measure how well a protein source meets human amino acid requirements. Whey scores close to 1.0 on PDCAAS. A good pea-rice blend scores approximately 0.8–0.9, which is meaningfully better than either source alone. Some manufacturers publish these scores — it is a good sign of transparency when they do.

**Third-party testing:** Protein powders are a supplement category with a well-documented history of label inaccuracy, contamination, and spiking — the practice of adding cheap amino acids like glycine or taurine to inflate the nitrogen content and therefore the apparent protein reading. Look for products certified by **Informed Sport, NSF Certified for Sport, or Labdoor**. These organisations independently test products and verify that what is on the label is actually in the product.

**Ingredient cleanliness:** The shorter the ingredient list, the better. Avoid products with excessive artificial sweeteners, fillers, or proprietary blends that obscure individual ingredient quantities. For a vegan client who is already eating a whole food diet, a clean powder that complements that approach is ideal.

**Taste and mixability:** This sounds trivial but it is not. A protein powder that the client does not enjoy drinking will not be used consistently, and consistency is everything. If possible, recommend she try sample sizes before committing to a large bag.

---

## Recommended Protein Types in Priority Order

### 1. Pea and Brown Rice Protein Blend — First Choice

This is the gold standard recommendation for vegan lifters and the type you should default to unless there is a specific reason not to. The combination of pea and rice protein produces an amino acid profile that closely rivals whey in completeness. Pea protein contributes strong lysine and arginine content; rice protein fills in the methionine and cysteine gaps that pea protein leaves. Together, at approximately a **70:30 or 80:20 pea-to-rice ratio**, the blend achieves a PDCAAS close to 1.0.

For this client, a pea-rice blend should be the everyday powder — used in the post-workout smoothie bowl (Meal 2 from the post-workout meal list), stirred into porridge, or blended into any meal where a protein boost is needed.

### 2. Soy Protein Isolate — Strong Alternative

Soy protein isolate is the only single-source plant protein that is genuinely complete — it scores approximately 0.98 on PDCAAS, essentially equivalent to whey. It is also high in leucine relative to other plant proteins and has decades of research supporting its use for muscle gain. For a long time there was concern about phytoestrogens in soy affecting hormonal balance, but the current body of evidence is clear: **moderate to high soy consumption does not negatively affect oestrogen levels or muscle building in women**, and the phytoestrogens in soy (isoflavones) are structurally very different from human oestrogen with much weaker receptor binding.

Soy protein isolate is a legitimate first choice, particularly if the client already eats a lot of whole soy foods like tofu, tempeh, and edamame, as the powder simply extends that pattern. The one consideration is variety — if she is already eating soy at multiple meals, rotating in a pea-rice blend ensures she is not over-relying on a single protein source.

### 3. Pea Protein Isolate — Good Single-Source Option

If a blend is not available or the client prefers a simpler product, pea protein isolate on its own is the best single-source vegan protein. It is high in BCAAs relative to other plant proteins, reasonably leucine-rich, and very well tolerated digestively. The main limitation is the methionine deficit, which can be partially addressed by ensuring other meals throughout the day contain methionine-rich foods such as hemp seeds, Brazil nuts, oats, and legumes. For a client eating a varied whole food diet, this gap is unlikely to be clinically significant.

### 4. Hemp Protein — Supplementary Use Only

Hemp protein is nutritionally interesting — it contains all nine essential amino acids and is rich in omega-3 fatty acids and fibre — but it is not a strong primary protein powder for muscle gain. The protein content per serving is lower (typically 12–15 g per 30 g serving), leucine content is poor, and the high fibre content can cause digestive discomfort in large quantities. Hemp protein is best used as a nutritional booster added to smoothies or porridge alongside a primary protein source, not as the main powder.

### 5. Sacha Inchi Protein — Emerging Option Worth Knowing

Sacha inchi is a seed from South America with a surprisingly complete amino acid profile and good leucine content. It is less widely available than pea or rice protein but is appearing in more vegan blends. If you come across a product featuring sacha inchi as part of a blend, it is a quality ingredient worth noting.

# Cheat Meal Day Guide

## Reframing the Concept First

Before prescribing a cheat meal day, it is worth having an honest conversation with the client — and with yourself as her trainer — about the language and psychology around this concept. The phrase "cheat meal" implies that eating certain foods is a moral failing that requires cheating to indulge in, which is not a healthy framework for someone who will be managing their nutrition for the long term. Many sports nutritionists and psychologists now prefer the terms **"free meal," "flex meal," or "planned indulgence"** for this reason.

That said, the practical concept is sound and well-supported by both physiology and behavioural psychology. A planned day of relaxed eating serves several legitimate purposes for this client specifically, and understanding those purposes will help both of you implement it intelligently rather than using it as an excuse to undermine the programme.

---

## Why a Flex Meal Day Is Actually Useful Here

**Physiological reasons:**

**Leptin resensitisation.** Leptin is the hormone primarily responsible for regulating hunger and metabolic rate. When eating in a caloric surplus for muscle gain, leptin levels are generally well maintained — but the psychological and physical fatigue of structured eating can still accumulate. A higher-calorie day periodically helps reinforce that the body is not in a state of scarcity, keeping metabolic rate and hormonal function optimal.

**Glycogen supercompensation.** A day with higher carbohydrate intake — which is almost inevitable on a flex meal day — can push muscle glycogen stores above their normal resting level. This means the client may actually train better in the day or two following a flex meal day, particularly if it falls before a heavy training session.

**Psychological sustainability.** This is arguably the most important reason of all. Strict dietary adherence seven days a week for twelve weeks is extremely difficult to maintain, and the research on dietary adherence is clear: **a plan followed at 85–90% consistency over twelve weeks produces far better results than a perfect plan followed for four weeks before being abandoned.** A planned flex day reduces the likelihood of unplanned, guilt-driven overeating and keeps the client engaged with the programme long term.

**Vegan-specific consideration.** Eating a strict vegan diet in social situations — restaurants, friends' homes, family gatherings — can already be socially isolating. A flex meal day gives the client permission to navigate social eating situations without stress, choosing the best vegan options available rather than feeling she has to bring her own food or decline invitations entirely.

---

## What a Flex Meal Day Is Not

It is important to set clear expectations so the flex day does not become a liability.

A flex meal day is **not** a day to eat until physically uncomfortable. It is **not** a reward for good behaviour during the week, because framing food as a reward creates an unhealthy psychological relationship with eating. It is **not** a day to abandon vegan principles — the client's ethical commitments do not have a day off. And it is **not** a day that should leave her feeling sluggish, bloated, or guilty the following morning.

The goal is **enjoyment within a loose structure** — not rigid tracking, but not complete abandonment of awareness either.

---

## When to Schedule the Flex Day

**Recommended: Saturday**

Saturday works best for several reasons. It is the furthest point from Monday's training session, giving the body time to process any excess sodium, water retention, or digestive load before the week's training begins. It also aligns naturally with social life — most social eating happens on weekends. The client is also not training on Sunday, so any mild digestive discomfort from richer food does not interfere with a gym session.

If Saturday does not suit her lifestyle, Sunday is the next best option. Avoid placing the flex day on Tuesday or Friday — the days immediately before or after heavy lower body sessions — because a very large meal can cause temporary bloating and discomfort that affects squat and deadlift performance.

**Frequency: Once per week throughout all three phases.**

Some programmes recommend a flex meal rather than a full flex day — one relaxed meal within an otherwise structured day. For a client in a muscle gain phase eating a caloric surplus, a full flex day is manageable without derailing progress, provided the guidelines below are followed. If at the four-week check-in weight is increasing faster than 0.5 kg per week, consider scaling back to a single flex meal rather than a full day.

---

## The Flex Day Structure

The flex day is not a free-for-all from the moment she wakes up. It has a loose structure that preserves some nutritional integrity while allowing genuine freedom.

---

### Morning — Keep It Normal

Start the day with a regular breakfast that resembles a typical programme day. This serves two purposes: it ensures she begins the day with adequate protein and nutrients rather than starting from zero, and it prevents the flex day from becoming a twelve-hour eating marathon that leaves her feeling terrible by evening.

**Suggested flex day breakfast:**
A normal meal from her existing rotation — the soy milk protein porridge, a tofu scramble, or a smoothie bowl. Something she enjoys and that delivers 30–40 g protein and a reasonable carbohydrate base. Have a coffee, enjoy the morning, and do not start thinking about the flex meal until lunchtime at the earliest.

---

### Midday — Transition Meal

Lunch on a flex day can be slightly more relaxed than a typical programme day but does not need to be the main event. This might be a vegan restaurant meal, a more indulgent homemade dish, or simply a larger portion of something she enjoys. She does not need to track this meal but should remain broadly aware of what she is eating.

**Ideas for a relaxed vegan lunch:**
- A large vegan burger with sweet potato fries at a restaurant
- Homemade vegan pizza on a thick base with generous toppings
- A big bowl of vegan ramen or pho
- Vegan sushi with edamame and miso soup
- A generous mezze spread with hummus, flatbreads, falafel, and dips

---

### Evening — The Main Flex Meal

This is the centrepiece of the flex day. The client should choose something she genuinely looks forward to — a meal that feels indulgent, satisfying, and enjoyable. The only non-negotiable is that it remains vegan.

**Guidelines for the main flex meal:**

- **Eat slowly and mindfully.** The flex day is about enjoyment, and enjoyment requires presence. Eating quickly while distracted reduces satisfaction and increases the likelihood of overeating past the point of comfort.
- **Stop when comfortably full, not stuffed.** This is not a competition. The goal is satisfaction, not maximum caloric intake.
- **Alcohol is a personal choice** but worth flagging: alcohol suppresses muscle protein synthesis for several hours after consumption and disrupts sleep quality significantly. If she chooses to drink, keeping it to one or two drinks and ensuring she is well hydrated will minimise the impact on recovery.
- **Dessert is absolutely fine.** Many vegan desserts are genuinely excellent — dark chocolate, fruit-based desserts, vegan ice cream, and baked goods made with plant-based ingredients are all fair game.

---

The following suggestions are organised by setting — home cooking, restaurant dining, and takeaway — to cover the range of situations she might find herself in on a Saturday.

---

### Home Cooking Flex Meals

**Vegan Loaded Nachos**
A genuinely indulgent sharing-style meal that works well for a Saturday evening at home. Tortilla chips layered with homemade refried black beans, vegan cheese (cashew-based melts best), guacamole, pico de gallo, pickled jalapeños, and vegan sour cream. Finish with fresh coriander and lime. This is high in carbohydrates and fat — exactly the kind of meal that feels like a treat — and it is entirely plant-based without any compromise.

**Vegan Mac and Cheese**
A comfort food classic. The best vegan mac and cheese uses a cashew and nutritional yeast sauce blended with roasted red pepper, garlic, and a splash of apple cider vinegar for tang. Baked in the oven with a breadcrumb topping until golden. Serve with a simple green salad to add some freshness and fibre. This is a meal that genuinely rivals the dairy version when made well, and it is worth encouraging the client to master this recipe as a go-to flex day dish.

**Vegan Burgers with All the Toppings**
Homemade black bean and beetroot burgers or store-bought premium vegan patties (Beyond Burger, Moving Mountains, or similar) in brioche-style vegan buns with lettuce, tomato, pickles, caramelised onions, vegan mayo, and mustard. Served with thick-cut oven fries or sweet potato wedges. A meal that is satisfying, familiar, and completely vegan.

**Vegan Curry Feast**
A spread of two or three different curries — perhaps a rich coconut-based tofu tikka masala, a saag aloo, and a dal makhani made with coconut cream — served with garlic naan (many shop-bought naans are accidentally vegan — check the label), basmati rice, mango chutney, and poppadoms. This style of meal is naturally high in carbohydrates and flavour, and the social, sharing nature of a curry feast makes it particularly enjoyable.

**Vegan Pasta Carbonara or Bolognese**
Pasta is one of the great comfort foods and works beautifully in a vegan context. A carbonara can be made with silken tofu blended with nutritional yeast, black pepper, and smoked paprika as the sauce, with smoked tempeh or coconut bacon as the pancetta substitute. A bolognese using lentils, walnuts, and mushrooms as the meat base is deeply satisfying and genuinely delicious. Serve with a generous portion of pasta — this is not a day for weighing it.

**Vegan Cheeseboard and Sharing Platter**
For a lighter but still indulgent flex meal, a vegan cheeseboard with a selection of artisan vegan cheeses (cashew brie, smoked almond cheese, and herb-crusted varieties are widely available), served with crackers, grapes, figs, olives, sun-dried tomatoes, hummus, and crusty bread. This works particularly well as a social meal shared with others.

---

### Restaurant Flex Meals

Eating out as a vegan has become significantly easier in recent years, and most cities now have dedicated vegan restaurants as well as mainstream restaurants with strong plant-based menus. Here is how to navigate different restaurant types on a flex day.

**Dedicated vegan restaurants:** The obvious first choice. No need to interrogate the menu or worry about cross-contamination. Order whatever appeals most — this is the flex day.

**Indian restaurants:** Naturally vegan-friendly. Dal, chana masala, aloo gobi, vegetable biryani, and many other dishes are vegan by default. Confirm that the naan is made without butter (ask for it without, or choose rice instead) and that the curries are not finished with cream or ghee.

**Japanese restaurants:** Vegetable sushi, edamame, miso soup, agedashi tofu (check the dashi stock — some use fish-based dashi, so ask), and vegetable ramen with a soy or miso broth are all good options. Many Japanese restaurants are accommodating of vegan requests.

**Italian restaurants:** Pasta with tomato-based sauces (marinara, arrabbiata, puttanesca without anchovies), bruschetta, and wood-fired vegetable pizzas without cheese (or with vegan cheese if available) are all solid choices. Ask the kitchen to confirm no egg in the pasta.

**Middle Eastern restaurants:** Falafel, hummus, baba ganoush, tabbouleh, stuffed vine leaves, and flatbreads make for an excellent and naturally vegan meal. One of the most reliably vegan-friendly cuisine types.

**Mexican restaurants:** Bean tacos, vegetable burritos, guacamole, and rice dishes are widely available. Confirm that the beans are not cooked with lard (a common practice in traditional Mexican cooking) and that sour cream and cheese are omitted or substituted.

---

### Takeaway Flex Meals

**Vegan pizza:** Most major pizza chains now offer vegan cheese and a range of plant-based toppings. Order a pizza she genuinely wants — extra toppings, thick crust, the works. This is the flex day.

**Vegan Chinese takeaway:** Tofu and vegetable dishes, spring rolls (check the wrapper — most are vegan), vegetable fried rice, and noodle dishes are widely available. Be aware that some Chinese sauces contain oyster sauce — ask for dishes to be made with soy sauce only.

**Vegan Indian takeaway:** As with restaurant dining, Indian takeaway is one of the most vegan-friendly options. Dal, chana masala, and vegetable curries with rice or naan are reliable choices.

**Vegan fast food:** The major fast food chains now have credible vegan options — plant-based burgers, wraps, and sides. Not the most nutritionally sophisticated choice but entirely appropriate for a flex day and genuinely enjoyable.

## What to Expect Physically After the Flex Day

It is important to prepare the client for the normal physiological responses to a flex day so she does not interpret them as fat gain or programme failure.

**Temporary weight increase:** She will almost certainly weigh more on Sunday morning than she did on Friday morning. This is not fat. A higher carbohydrate intake causes the body to store more glycogen, and each gram of glycogen is stored with approximately 3 g of water. A flex day with an extra 150–200 g of carbohydrates above normal can cause 0.5–1.5 kg of temporary water weight gain. This resolves within 48–72 hours as glycogen is used during training. Advise her not to weigh herself on Sunday morning — or if she does, to understand exactly what she is seeing.

**Possible bloating:** Richer, higher-fat foods slow gastric emptying. Some vegan flex meal options — particularly those high in legumes, cruciferous vegetables, or novel ingredients — may cause temporary bloating. This is normal and resolves quickly. Staying well hydrated on Sunday helps.

**Potentially better training on Monday or Tuesday:** As mentioned earlier, the glycogen supercompensation effect of a higher-carbohydrate day often translates to improved performance in the gym in the following one to two days. Encourage her to notice this — it reinforces the positive relationship between the flex day and her training rather than framing it as something she needs to recover from.

---

## The Day After — Sunday Reset

Sunday is a full rest day. No specific nutritional intervention is needed — simply return to the normal programme eating pattern. There is no need to restrict calories, do extra cardio, or compensate in any way for the flex day. Compensation behaviour is psychologically harmful and physiologically unnecessary. One higher-calorie day within a week of structured eating in a modest surplus will not derail twelve weeks of progress.

**Sunday nutrition:** Return to normal meal structure. Hit the 150 g protein target. Drink plenty of water. Eat whole foods. That is all.

# Phase 3 Intensification — Updated and Expanded

## Why Push Harder in Phase 3

The first eight weeks of this programme have done two critical things: they have built a substantial base of training volume that has driven meaningful hypertrophy, and they have prepared the client's muscles, connective tissue, and nervous system to handle significantly higher intensities without breaking down. Phase 3 is where that preparation pays off. The body has adapted to the stimulus of Phases 1 and 2 — if intensity stays the same, adaptation slows. The only way to continue driving muscle growth in the final four weeks is to push harder than the body has experienced before.

This updated Phase 3 is more demanding than the version in the original programme. The techniques introduced here — mechanical drop sets, cluster sets, myo-reps, forced eccentrics, and intraset stretching — are not gimmicks. Each one has a specific physiological rationale for why it drives hypertrophy beyond what straight sets can achieve at this stage of the programme. Explain each technique to the client before she encounters it in a session so she understands what she is doing and why, rather than simply following instructions.

**A clear warning before proceeding:** Higher intensity means higher recovery demand. Everything said earlier in the programme about sleep, nutrition, and stress management becomes even more critical in Phase 3. If the client is not sleeping at least seven to eight hours, not hitting her protein target consistently, and not managing life stress reasonably well, pushing intensity this high will produce diminishing returns at best and overreaching at worst. Assess her recovery status honestly before implementing this phase.

---

## Intensity Techniques Used in Phase 3

Before the weekly sessions are laid out, each technique is explained in full so you can coach them correctly.

---

### Mechanical Drop Sets

A mechanical drop set changes the **mechanical advantage** rather than the weight, allowing more reps to be performed as the muscle fatigues by moving to a position where the target muscle is stronger. Unlike a traditional drop set where you reduce the load, a mechanical drop set keeps the load the same and changes the exercise or body position.

**Example on the dumbbell lateral raise:**
Perform 10 reps of a standard lateral raise to failure. Without resting, switch immediately to a partial range lateral raise (lifting only from hip height to just below shoulder height — the strongest portion of the movement). Perform as many reps as possible. Without resting, switch to a cable lateral raise or lean slightly forward to change the line of pull and squeeze out further reps. The deltoid is taken well beyond the point of failure it would reach in a straight set, creating a much stronger hypertrophic stimulus.

**Example on the leg press:**
Perform 12 reps at full range to near failure. Without resting, reduce range of motion to the top half of the movement (where the quads are in a mechanically stronger position) and perform 8 more reps. Without resting, reduce to quarter reps and perform as many as possible. The quad is under continuous tension and metabolic stress far beyond what a straight set achieves.

---

### Cluster Sets

A cluster set breaks a traditional set into mini-sets separated by very short intraset rest periods of 10–20 seconds. This allows the client to use a heavier load than she could sustain for a continuous set of the same total reps, because the brief rest periods allow partial phosphocreatine resynthesis without allowing full recovery.

**Example:** Instead of 4 × 8 on the barbell bench press at a given weight, perform 4 × (4 + 4) with 15 seconds rest between the two mini-sets. The load used can be approximately 5–10% heavier than the straight set equivalent, meaning the muscle is exposed to greater mechanical tension — the primary driver of hypertrophy — for the same total rep count.

Cluster sets are best used on compound movements where load is the primary variable. They are not necessary on isolation exercises where metabolic stress and pump are the goals.

---

### Myo-Reps

Myo-reps are an advanced technique developed by Norwegian strength coach Børge Fagerli. The concept is based on the observation that the most hypertrophically effective reps in any set are the final few — the ones performed closest to muscular failure, where the greatest number of motor units are recruited. Myo-reps are designed to accumulate a high number of these effective reps in a short time.

**How to perform myo-reps:**
1. Perform an activation set of 12–15 reps, taking the set to within one or two reps of failure. This pre-fatigues the muscle and ensures maximum motor unit recruitment.
2. Rack the weight and rest for exactly 3–5 deep breaths (approximately 20–30 seconds).
3. Perform 3–5 reps. Rack again.
4. Rest 3–5 breaths.
5. Perform 3–5 reps. Rack again.
6. Continue until you can no longer complete the minimum rep count (3 reps) with good form.

A typical myo-rep set might look like: 15 reps, rest, 5 reps, rest, 4 reps, rest, 4 reps, rest, 3 reps, rest, 3 reps — stop. That is 34 total reps, the vast majority of which were performed in a high-fatigue state with near-complete motor unit recruitment. The hypertrophic stimulus is significantly greater than a standard 3 × 12 at the same load.

Myo-reps work best on isolation exercises and machine-based movements where form is easy to maintain under fatigue — leg extensions, cable rows, lateral raises, bicep curls, and leg curls are ideal candidates.

---

### Forced Eccentrics (Eccentric Overload)

The eccentric phase of a lift — the lowering phase — produces greater muscle damage and hypertrophic stimulus than the concentric phase. Muscles can handle approximately 20–40% more load eccentrically than concentrically, meaning there is significant untapped stimulus available if eccentrics are emphasised.

**Tempo manipulation:** The simplest form of eccentric overload is slowing the lowering phase to 4–6 seconds on key exercises. This increases time under tension dramatically and causes significantly greater muscle damage than a normal tempo.

**Partner-assisted forced eccentrics:** On exercises like the barbell curl or leg curl, the client performs the concentric phase normally, then the trainer applies gentle additional resistance during the eccentric phase — enough to make the lowering significantly harder without causing form breakdown. This technique should only be used on exercises where the trainer can safely apply and remove resistance, and only on the final one or two sets of an exercise when the client is already well warmed up.

**1.5 rep method:** Perform a full rep, return halfway, pause, return to the bottom, then complete the full rep again. This counts as one repetition. The target muscle spends significantly more time in the stretched position — which research increasingly suggests is one of the most potent positions for hypertrophic stimulus — and the eccentric load is effectively doubled.

---

### Intraset Stretching (Stretch-Mediated Hypertrophy)

Recent research has highlighted that performing exercises through a full range of motion — particularly emphasising the stretched position — produces greater hypertrophy than partial range training. Intraset stretching takes this further by incorporating a deliberate pause in the fully stretched position during each rep.

**Example on the dumbbell Romanian deadlift:**
At the bottom of each rep, pause for 2–3 seconds in the fully stretched hamstring position before driving back up. The combination of load and stretch in this position creates significant mechanical tension in the muscle at its longest length, which appears to be a particularly powerful hypertrophic stimulus.

**Example on the incline dumbbell curl:**
The incline position already places the bicep in a stretched position at the bottom of the movement. Add a 2-second pause at the bottom of each rep to maximise this effect.

**Example on the cable fly:**
At the fully open position — arms wide, chest maximally stretched — pause for 2 seconds before bringing the arms together. This is uncomfortable but highly effective.

---

### Rest-Pause Sets

Already introduced briefly in Phase 2, rest-pause sets are used more aggressively in Phase 3. Take a set to technical failure, rack the weight, rest 15–20 seconds, then perform as many additional reps as possible. Repeat once more if the client can manage it. This extends a single set well beyond normal failure, accumulating additional effective reps without the time cost of a full additional set.

## Updated Phase 3 Sessions

### Week 9

---

**Monday — Upper Body A (Push Focus)**

Warm-up: 8 minutes on the rowing machine at easy pace, followed by band pull-aparts (3 × 15), arm circles, and thoracic rotations. Do not skip the warm-up in Phase 3 — the intensity of the working sets makes adequate preparation non-negotiable.

**Barbell Bench Press — Cluster Sets**
4 sets of (5 + 5) with 15 seconds intraset rest between the two mini-sets. Use a load approximately 7–8% heavier than the straight set weight used in Phase 2. Rest 2.5 minutes between cluster sets. RPE on the second mini-set of each cluster should be 8–9. Focus on a controlled 3-second eccentric on every rep — do not let the bar drop.

**Incline Dumbbell Press — 1.5 Rep Method**
3 sets × 8 full reps using the 1.5 rep method. Lower the dumbbells to the fully stretched position, press halfway up, lower back to the stretch, then press to full lockout — that is one rep. The pectoral stretch at the bottom is the target. Rest 2 minutes. RPE 8.

**Cable Chest Fly — Myo-Reps with Intraset Stretch**
1 activation set of 15 reps, pausing 2 seconds in the fully stretched position on every rep. Then myo-rep clusters of 4 reps with 5-breath rest periods until 4 reps cannot be completed. Rest 90 seconds after the full myo-rep sequence before moving on. This will create an intense pump in the pectorals — that is the goal.

**Dumbbell Overhead Press — Mechanical Drop Set**
3 sets. Perform 10 reps of a standard overhead press to near failure. Without resting, immediately switch to a lateral raise with the same dumbbells and perform as many reps as possible. Without resting, perform front raises to failure. Rest 90 seconds between each mechanical drop set. The deltoid is hit from three angles in rapid succession with no rest.

**Tricep Pushdown (rope) — Rest-Pause**
3 sets to technical failure, followed immediately by a 20-second rest and then as many additional reps as possible. Rest 60 seconds between sets. Keep elbows pinned throughout — as fatigue accumulates the temptation to flare the elbows increases.

**Lateral Raise (cable) — Forced Eccentric**
3 sets × 10 reps with a 4-second eccentric on every rep. Use a lighter load than normal to accommodate the slower tempo — the time under tension is the stimulus here, not the load. Rest 60 seconds.

**Tuesday — Lower Body A (Quad Focus)**

Warm-up: 10 minutes incline treadmill walk, followed by bodyweight squats (2 × 15), leg swings, hip circles, and glute bridges (2 × 15).

**Barbell Back Squat — Cluster Sets**
5 sets of (4 + 3) with 20 seconds intraset rest. Use a load 5–8% heavier than the straight set weight from Phase 2. Rest 3 minutes between cluster sets. The squat is the most technically demanding exercise in the programme — do not sacrifice depth or spinal position for load. If form breaks down, reduce the load immediately. RPE on the second mini-set should be 9.

**Bulgarian Split Squat — 1.5 Rep Method with Intraset Stretch**
4 sets × 8 reps each leg using the 1.5 rep method. Lower to the fully stretched position, rise halfway, lower back to the stretch, then stand fully — one rep. The hip flexor and quad stretch at the bottom is intense. Pause 2 seconds at the bottom of each full rep. Rest 2 minutes between sets. This exercise will be significantly harder than it was in Phase 2 — reduce the load if necessary to maintain the full range.

**Leg Press — Mechanical Drop Set**
3 sets. Perform 12 reps at full range to near failure. Without resting, reduce to half range (top portion) and perform 8 reps. Without resting, reduce to quarter reps and perform as many as possible. Rest 2.5 minutes between mechanical drop sets. The quad burn during this exercise will be severe — this is normal and expected.

**Leg Extension — Myo-Reps with Forced Eccentric**
1 activation set of 15 reps with a 3-second eccentric on every rep. Then myo-rep clusters of 4 reps (maintaining the 3-second eccentric) with 5-breath rest periods until 4 reps cannot be completed with the slow eccentric. Rest 90 seconds. The combination of myo-reps and forced eccentrics on this exercise creates an extraordinary amount of mechanical tension and metabolic stress in the quad — it is one of the most effective quad isolation techniques available.

**Standing Calf Raise — Rest-Pause with Intraset Stretch**
4 sets to failure, followed by 15-second rest and additional reps. On every rep, pause 3 seconds at the bottom in the fully stretched position before rising. Calves are notoriously stubborn and respond well to high volume, stretch emphasis, and extended sets. Rest 45 seconds between sets.

**Thursday — Upper Body B (Pull Focus)**

Warm-up: 8 minutes rowing machine, band pull-aparts (3 × 15), scapular retractions, and dead hangs from the pull-up bar (3 × 20 seconds).

4 sets of (3 + 3) with 20 seconds intraset rest. Add weight via a dipping belt or weighted vest. 4 sets × 8 reps with a 4-second eccentric on every rep. Lower the bar with complete control, feeling the lats lengthen under load. This is significantly harder than it sounds — reduce the load by approximately 15–20% compared to the normal working weight to accommodate the tempo. Rest 2 minutes.

**Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row — Myo-Reps**
1 activation set of 15 reps. Then myo-rep clusters of 4 reps with 5-breath rest periods. The chest-supported position eliminates lower back fatigue, meaning the lats and rhomboids can be taken to true failure without the lower back giving out first. This is important in Phase 3 when the goal is genuine muscular failure rather than systemic fatigue.

**Single-Arm Cable Row — 1.5 Rep Method with Intraset Stretch**
3 sets × 10 reps each arm. Row to full contraction, return halfway, pause 2 seconds in the fully stretched position (arm extended, lat lengthened), return to full contraction, then lower fully — one rep. The stretch pause is the key element here. Rest 90 seconds between sets.

**Incline Dumbbell Curl — Myo-Reps with Intraset Stretch**
1 activation set of 12 reps, pausing 2 seconds at the bottom of every rep in the fully stretched bicep position. Then myo-rep clusters of 3 reps (maintaining the stretch pause) with 5-breath rest periods. The incline position places the bicep in a stretched position throughout the movement — combined with myo-reps, this is one of the most effective bicep techniques in the programme.

3 sets to failure followed by 15-second rest and additional reps. Keep the external rotation emphasis throughout — this exercise is as much about shoulder health as it is about rear deltoid development, and that function should not be sacrificed for load or reps.

2 sets. Perform 12 reps of a standard rear delt fly to near failure. Without resting, switch to a bent-over dumbbell rear delt fly (different line of pull) and perform as many reps as possible. Rest 60 seconds.

**Friday — Lower Body B (Posterior Chain Focus)**

Warm-up: 10 minutes easy bike, followed by glute bridges (2 × 20), leg swings, hip flexor stretches, and Romanian deadlift with empty bar (2 × 10 focusing on hamstring stretch).
